Political economy. The study of how political institutions, power structures, and economic systems interact and mutually shape one another. Rather than treating economics and politics as separate domains, political economy recognizes that markets are embedded in political frameworks, that governments regulate exchange, and that economic interests drive political conflict. Emerging as formal analysis in the eighteenth century with thinkers like Adam Smith, it remains essential for understanding how societies organize production and distribution.

The term political economy originated in the eighteenth century as economists and philosophers recognized that economic activity occurred within political systems and was shaped by laws, taxes, and government power. Adam Smith, though associated with free markets, analyzed how economic behavior depended on social institutions. He was a political economist, not a market-fundamentalist ideologue.

Classical political economists—David Ricardo, Thomas Malthus, John Stuart Mill—all analyzed how distribution of wealth depended on class-based power relationships, not just supply and demand. Karl Marx developed the most systematic political-economic analysis, arguing that economic systems—capitalism, feudalism, and others—determined political and cultural structures, not merely shaped them. A materialist view of history.

Comparative political economy examines how different nations organize production and distribution. Capitalism, socialism, mercantilism, and mixed economies represent different political-economic arrangements. Modern political economy addresses how states regulate markets, manage financial systems, set tariffs, and negotiate trade—recognizing that the market is a political creation, not a natural force.

Institutional analysis in political economy examines how different rules and structures shape economic outcomes. Property law, banking systems, labor regulations. The same technology produces different results in different institutional contexts. Political economy relates closely to power, the central political dimension political economy incorporates into economic analysis, to Adam Smith, the founding figure of modern political economy and economics, and to policy, the practical application of political-economic analysis in government decision-making.
